title: Movements, closed
hookLine: old schools and new movements, each in its own words

lines: A RAFT OF GRASS AND BRANCHES.
cards: A traveler crosses a river on a raft he has lashed together from grass and branches. On the far bank he stops. This raft served me well, he thinks.

Should I carry it on my head from now on? In the Buddha's parable, told in full on day four twenty, the answer is no: a raft is for crossing, not for carrying. The Buddha said his teaching was like that raft.
These last weeks brought a great many rafts, old and new, built in many countries from many kinds of wood.

teach.b: First, the Chinese schools. Tiantai, the Lotus school, with its three truths and its calming and seeing. Huayan, the flower garland, where everything holds everything else, like Fazang's lion, gold in every hair.
Tendai on the mother mountain. Shingon, the true word, its two mandalas and the letter A.
Then Nichiren and the title of the Lotus Sutra, its written mandala, and the many communities that chant it, each speaking for itself.
Third, old roots and new branches. Newar Buddhism in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley, with its householder priests.

Then movements of recent times: Goenka's ten-day silent courses, the insight movement, Won Buddhism and its circle, Triratna, Navayana with Ambedkar's followers, and Secular Buddhism, with others who disagree.
Fourth, practice put to work. Engaged Buddhism, in hard places. Humanistic Buddhism in Taiwan, and its relief volunteers.
The family altar. Communities living together. Zen centers far from home.
Some of these schools disagree with each other, sometimes sharply, about texts, practice, authority and what awakening is.

Each has described itself here in its own words, unranked, and the next block works the same way: starting tomorrow, the schools side by side, what they share and where they really differ, without crowning a winner.
In the parable, the teaching is for crossing over. Each movement met here is a different answer to one question: how do people, in this place and time, build something that floats?

how: Buddhists belong to many schools and movements, from old Chinese and Japanese schools to modern lay and engaged movements, and each explains its practice and teaching in its own words.

games.q: a friend has heard you've been learning about Buddhist schools. they ask: so which one is the real Buddhism? what do you say?
o: say each explains itself, and let them describe their own way.
games.why: this course lets each school speak for itself. the next block sets them side by side, without crowning a winner.

practice: Picture a slow river and breathe with it, letting the names from these weeks drift past like rafts: Tiantai, Huayan, Tendai, Shingon, Nichiren, Newar, the ten-day course, insight, Won, Triratna, Navayana, secular, engaged, humanistic, relief, the family altar, communities, Zen in the West.
Don't hold on to any of them; just notice which one your attention turns toward, a temple, a course, a community you'd like to see for yourself. Let that one stay a moment.

wordCard.voice: Movements. The schools and communities of Buddhism, old and new, each with its own practice and its own way of explaining itself. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: many ways. Every raft is for crossing, not for carrying. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Alagaddupama Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 22), the parable of the raft
